content: Cutaneous horns, also referred to by their Latin name cornu cutaneum, are rare keratinous skin tumors that resemble horns, and in some cases, they may appear similar to wood or coral. Clinically, they are defined as a conical projection above the surface of the skin. These growths are typically small and localized, but in very rare instances, they can grow to a much larger size. While they are often benign, they may also be malignant or premalignant. The exact cause of cutaneous horns remains unknown. However, it is believed that exposure to radiation, particularly ultraviolet radiation from sunlight, may play a role in their development. This is supported by the observation that these lesions are more commonly found on areas of the body frequently exposed to sunlight, such as the face and hands. Additionally, some cases have reported the development of cutaneous horns from burn scars. A potential association with the human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly the HPV-2 subtype, has also been suggested, as is the case with many other wart-like skin conditions. Prominent cases of cutaneous horns include Zhang Ruifang, a 101-year-old woman from Linlou Village in Henan Province, China, who developed a horn on her forehead. This growth, which has been described as resembling Devil's Horns, has reached a length of 6 centimeters. Another horn is reportedly forming on the opposite side of her forehead. Another notable case is that of Huang Yuanfan, an 84-year-old individual from Ziyuan, China, who also developed a cutaneous horn. Historical records also mention a woman who had an 8-inch horn removed from her forehead by French surgeon Dr. Joseph Souberbielle (1754–1846). A wax model of her head is displayed at the Mütter Museum in Philadelphia, USA. In terms of mortality and morbidity, the lesion at the base of the keratin mound is benign in the majority of cases. However, malignancy is present in up to 20% of cases, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most common type. The risk of squamous cell carcinoma increases to 37% when the cutaneous horn is located on the penis. Tenderness at the base of the lesion is often an indicator of a possible underlying squamous cell carcinoma. The diagnosis of cutaneous horns is primarily clinical and involves a thorough physical examination. Visual inspection and palpation of the lesion are essential to assess its characteristics and determine the need for further investigation or intervention. Treatment of cutaneous horns involves the removal of the keratinous growth, which is composed of the same material as fingernails, using a sterile razor. However, addressing the underlying condition that caused the horn is crucial. Treatment options may include surgical excision, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, depending on the nature of the underlying pathology.
